analysis.one_liner: Sets federal standards for managed care plans and requires health plans to give patients real choice of coverage.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 1994 with one Democratic and one Republican sponsor, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Secretary of Health and Human Services to certify managed care plans and the companies that review medical claims, with standards forcing plans to disclose how they pay doctors to limit care, guarantee timely access to physicians including in rural areas, and give patients and doctors due process when care is denied [S2] [S3]. It would have barred prior authorization for emergency care, required answers to authorization requests within 24 hours, and let denied patients appeal to independent reviewers [S3]. Every employer or plan sponsor would have had to offer enrollees a menu of plans including at least one traditional fee-for-service plan, and plans restricting doctors would have had to offer out-of-network point-of-service coverage [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Patients enrolled in managed care plans, who would gain plain-language disclosure of plan limits and of financial incentives that pay doctors to withhold services, guaranteed physician access, emergency care without prior approval, and independent appeals of denied claims [S3]. Physicians would gain due-process rights before losing plan credentials and review only by same-specialty doctors [S3]. Enrollees with incomes up to 200 percent of the federal poverty line would pay no more than in-plan limits for out-of-network care [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Managed care patients and their doctors

how_it_helps.text: Managed care plans would have to disclose coverage terms, financial incentives not to provide services, loss ratios, and enrollee satisfaction statistics in standardized, comparable form [S3].
No prior authorization for emergency care, 24-hour answers on other authorization requests, and a rule that care is deemed approved if reviewers are unavailable [S3].

Patients and doctors whose claims are denied as not medically necessary would get an appeal to a reviewer independent of the entity that made the initial denial, and anyone denying care must be a licensed professional of the same specialty [S3].

Each plan sponsor, including self-insured employers, would have to offer a choice of plans including a traditional fee-for-service option, and plans restricting provider networks would have to offer point-of-service out-of-network coverage with coinsurance capped at 20 percent [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Managed care plans and insurers would bear the cost of federal certification, disclosure, reserve, and appeal requirements, and employers or plan sponsors would bear the cost of offering a wider menu of plans [S3]. Some of those costs would likely flow to premiums paid by employers and enrollees, since the bill requires plan offerings beyond cheapest managed-care-only options [S3].

drawbacks.text: The choice mandate would require every sponsor to offer at least one traditional fee-for-service plan where available, which typically costs more than managed care, raising premiums or employer benefit costs [S3].

Rules such as deeming services approved when review staff are unavailable and capping coinsurance at 20 percent for out-of-network care would raise plan costs, and a federal certification bureaucracy could add administrative burden for plans [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections target real practices of the early-1990s managed care boom: undisclosed incentives for doctors to limit care, opaque denials, and no meaningful appeal. Those gains are concrete for patients. The trade-off is higher premiums and administrative costs, since guaranteed choice of traditional plans and looser utilization review push against the cost control that managed care was sold on. The bill never advanced far enough for these trade-offs to be tested or amended.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-June 1994 and referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which never held a markup or vote before the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995 [S5].

narrative.text: Senator Paul Wellstone, joined by Senator Burns, introduced the Patient Protection Act of 1994 on June 15, 1994, and spoke about it on the Senate floor [S3] [S5].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S5].
No further action was ever recorded: the bill received no subcommittee or full committee consideration, no floor vote, and the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Managed care plans and utilization review companies, which continued operating without federal certification standards, disclosure of their financial incentives, or independent appeal requirements.

for.name: Paul Wellstone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Patient Protection Act of 1994 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor [S3] [S5].

for.name: Conrad Burns
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it bipartisan from introduction [S4].

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill; it was referred on June 15, 1994 and received no markup, hearing action, or vote before the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat (Wellstone) sponsored and a Republican (Burns) cosponsored, but no committee or floor votes were ever recorded, so no partisan split can be measured [S3] [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have subjected them to federal certification: disclosing financial incentives not to provide services, loss ratios, and denial criteria; guaranteeing physician access including in rural areas; and limiting prior authorization. It also would have given certified plans a federal stamp of legitimacy, but the binding constraints fell on their cost-control and denial practices, which is where their interest ran against patients' [S3].
The choice mandate would have required every plan sponsor to offer at least one traditional fee-for-service plan, steering enrollment toward these insurers' products [S3].

Doctors would have gained due-process rights before losing credentials, same-specialty reviewers for denied care, protection from unadjusted economic profiling, and defined input into plan medical policy [S3].

Sponsors, including self-insured employers, would have had to offer a wider menu of plans and comply with disclosure requirements, adding administrative and premium costs even though employees would gain choice [S3].
